_comment: Reflective writing generation content, shared by life-timeline (mode=life-story) and memory-journal-prompt (mode=journal). The journal theme is never looked up in a table: whatever the author picked or typed is interpolated into the prompt, so presets and custom themes take one path. Edit wording here rather than in studio_life_timeline_service.py.

lifeStory._comment: stageLabels turn the config key into words a model can write about — the request carries 'youngAdult', the prompt must say 'young adulthood'. stageLenses say what makes a memory belong to this stage and nowhere else; stageAnchors are the phrases that mark the time without every prompt parroting the page header. stageHints are the raw material a prompt writer would reach for: specific enough that the model does not fall back to 'home, family, play'.

stageLabels.places: places lived in and journeys taken
stageLabels.timeline: a whole life, one line at a time

stageLenses.childhood: the world at a child's height — what the grown-ups decided, what was done without any money, what felt enormous at the time
stageLenses.school: the years of being a pupil — bells and lessons, the playground, being one of a class, walking or riding there and back
stageLenses.youngAdult: the first years of answering to nobody — your own wage, your own room, going out, learning to manage things yourself
stageLenses.work: the years of earning a living — the workplace itself, the people in it, the trade or knack you were known for
stageLenses.family: the years your household and your circle were busiest — gatherings, traditions, the people who called in
stageLenses.places: the towns, houses and journeys — arriving somewhere new, settling in, the route you knew best, going back
stageLenses.laterLife: the years the days became your own — unhurried mornings, younger visitors, long-practised routines
stageLenses.timeline: any single point across a whole life, each cue clearly placed in its own time

lifeStory.customStageLens: what could only have happened during "{stage}" and at no other point in a life

childhood: in the school holidays when you were young
at the age when the grown-ups decided everything
school: at the school you went to
in the year you liked best at school
youngAdult: in your late teens and twenties
when you first had money of your own
in the years you first went out on your own
when you first lived away from where you grew up
work: at the place you worked longest
when you were still new to the job
family: in the years your house was busiest
in the years you saw most of your neighbours and friends
places: in the place you lived longest
when you first arrived somewhere new
on the journey you made most often
laterLife: now the days are your own
since you stopped keeping to anyone else's clock
timeline: at that point in your life

stageHints.childhood: the house and who was in it, the yard or street outside, games nobody organised, sweets and Sunday food, pets, bedtime, hand-me-down clothes, weather and seasons
stageHints.school: the journey there and back, the classroom and the playground, a teacher's habits and sayings, lessons loved and dreaded, lunches, uniforms, nicknames, the sound of the bell
stageHints.youngAdult: the first wage and what it bought, a first room of one's own, music and dancing, clothes and hair, going out with friends, buses and bicycles, learning to cook, drive or mend things
stageHints.work: the first morning at a new job, tools, desks and machines, workmates and their sayings, tea breaks, what the place smelled and sounded like, a skill they became known for, payday
stageHints.family: birthdays and weddings, family sayings and traditions, neighbours who called in, cooking for a crowd, who made everyone laugh, holidays at home, the photographs taken
stageHints.places: streets and houses lived in, the journey to get there, the view from a window, seaside and countryside days, packing up and moving, a place they went back to again and again
stageHints.laterLife: hobbies picked back up, young visitors, the garden, a well-practised recipe, a favourite chair and what was on, walks and neighbours, the quiet pleasures of an ordinary day
stageHints.timeline: short one-line memory cues that could sit anywhere across a whole life

lifeStory.customStageHint: the ordinary texture of "{stage}" — the people around them, where they were, what they did on an ordinary day, and the sounds, smells, food and objects that belonged to it
avoidTopics: death, bereavement, illness, injury, or care needs
regret, failure, mistakes, or "what would you do differently"
anything judging whether their life was well spent
exact years, dates, ages, full names or addresses — nothing that puts the reader's memory on trial
anything that assumes the reader had siblings, children, a partner, a car, a holiday or spare money — ask openly, so anyone can answer
anything requiring a yes/no answer, or starting with {yes_no_openers}

journal._comment: Journal prompts are printed one to a page, so each has to stand alone. No table lookup for themes: whatever the author picked or typed is interpolated into themeHint, so presets and custom themes take one path. timeFrames is the whole of the 'when' instruction — it drops into the template as one block, so each entry carries its own anchoring language rather than a bare label.
journal.themeHint: "{theme}" — every prompt must clearly fit this theme, as an ordinary reader would understand those words, and each prompt must reach a different corner of it
journal.openThemeHint: a bit of everything — no single subject, so spread the prompts across ordinary life: people, places, food and home, work and hobbies, the senses, and the small pleasures of a day

timeFrames.past: When: earlier life. Anchor every prompt in the past — "when you were younger", "in the house you grew up in", "back when" — and keep the memories warm ones. Never ask about today.
timeFrames.present: When: today and this week. Ask about what is within reach now — this morning, the view from the window, what was on the table, who called in. Low-pressure: nothing to work out, nothing to look up.
timeFrames.future: When: the days ahead. Ask about something small and gentle to look forward to, plan, or wish for. Keep it within an ordinary week at home — never anything that depends on health, money, or travelling far.
timeFrames.mixed: When: vary it across the set — some prompts about earlier life, some about today or this week, and at least one about something to look forward to. Never two in a row from the same time frame.

avoidTopics: death, bereavement, illness, injury, or care needs
regret, failure, mistakes, or "what would you do differently"
exact years, dates, ages, full names or addresses — nothing that puts the reader's memory on trial
how much they remember, or anything they can no longer do — never measure the reader against a younger self
anything that assumes the reader had siblings, children, a partner, a car, a holiday or spare money — ask openly, so anyone can answer
anything requiring a yes/no answer, or starting with {yes_no_openers}
